<div><div class="book-report__eyebrow">Book review · Buddhist art history · trans-Asian exchange · Tang · Nara · Grand Silla</div><h1>Buddhist Pilgrim-Monks as Agents of Cultural and Artistic Transmission</h1><p class="book-report__author">The International Buddhist Art Style in East Asia, ca. 645–770<br>Dorothy C. Wong</p>
<dl class="book-report__meta" aria-label="Bibliographic reference"><div><dt>Date</dt><dd>2018</dd></div><div><dt>Publisher</dt><dd>NUS Press · National University of Singapore</dd></div><div><dt>Language</dt><dd>English</dd></div><div><dt>Field</dt><dd>Buddhist art history · trans-Asian exchange · Tang · Nara · Grand Silla</dd></div><div><dt>Type</dt><dd>Scholarly monograph</dd></div><div><dt>Reference</dt><dd>ISBN 978-981-4722-59-9</dd></div></dl>
<div class="book-report__domain"><strong>Central question:</strong> How did an “international” Buddhist visual language form, circulate and change between India, China, the Korean Peninsula and Japan ca. 645–770, and what roles did traveling monks, great monasteries and courts play in that process?</div>
</div></div></header>
<div class="book-report__nav-wrap"><nav class="book-report__shell book-report__nav" aria-label="Review contents">
<a href="#pourquoi-lire">Why read it?</a><a href="#comprendre">What it helps us understand</a><a href="#apports">Contributions</a><a href="#reperes">Key references</a><a href="#these">Author’s thesis</a><a href="#changement">What it changes</a><a href="#limites">Limits</a><a href="#public">For whom?</a><a href="#verdict">Verdict</a>
</nav></div>

<section class="book-report__section" id="pourquoi-lire"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">01 · Essential</div><h2>Why read this book?</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p>This book matters because it replaces the vague language of “influence” with an investigation of the concrete mechanisms of artistic circulation. Dorothy C. Wong does not only ask where a form came from: she asks who carried it, through which institutional networks, together with which texts, rituals, objects and skills, and how it was altered in a new setting. Pilgrim-monks therefore become art-historical actors alongside patrons, artisans and monuments.</p><p>For Buddhist art history, the payoff is substantial. Xuanzang (玄奘), Dōji (道慈) and Jianzhen (鑑真) appear as mediators who moved images, relics, architectural models, ordination practices and iconographic programs. The book connects Bodhgayā, Chang’an, Luoyang, Nara and, more selectively, Grand Silla. Above all, it shows that a style becomes “international” only when several societies adopt, adapt and reinterpret it.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="comprendre"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">02 · Knowledge</div><h2>What the book helps us understand</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><ul class="book-report__keypoints"><li><strong>An “international style” is not simply a Chinese export.</strong> The visual language studied here combines Indian and Central Asian inheritances with forms developed in the Tang capitals, then circulates through China, Korea and Japan.</li><li><strong>Monks are material agents of art.</strong> They transmit more than doctrine: they carry texts, relics and images, supervise monasteries, guide commissions and introduce ritual and technical practices.</li><li><strong>Great monasteries are network nodes.</strong> They produce, authenticate, preserve and circulate texts, rituals and artworks while linking courts, workshops, monastic communities and travelers.</li><li><strong>Court art and Buddhist state ideology are closely connected.</strong> Buddhist kingship, the cakravartin model and Avataṃsaka cosmology give visual form to the ambitions of Wu Zhao and later Shōmu and Kōmyō.</li><li><strong>Transmission always involves transformation.</strong> An image, monastery plan or practice can be relocated and then reinterpreted locally; Wong therefore favors a “transmission-transformation” model over a fixed center-periphery relationship.</li></ul></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="apports"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">03 · Perspective</div><h2>Contributions to art history, Buddhism and Asian history</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p><strong>For art history</strong>, the book offers a method for tracing forms across borders. It combines stylistic analysis, iconography, architecture, materiality, ritual and the biographies of agents. The Bodhgayā Buddha in earth-touching gesture, mold-pressed clay tablets, the bejeweled Buddha, Vairocana programs and Avalokiteśvara images become cases of circulation rather than isolated motifs.</p><p><strong>For Buddhist studies</strong>, Wong stresses the direct involvement of clerics in image worship, relic cults, ritual, ordination and construction. Learned Buddhism and material culture are not separate realms: translation, theories of the Buddha’s bodies, dhāraṇīs, protective rites and monuments are produced within overlapping networks.</p><p><strong>For Asian history</strong>, the book gives a powerful account of seventh- and eighth-century cosmopolitanism. Official missions, international monastic communities, court workshops, great monasteries and mobile craftspeople form a transregional infrastructure through which ideas and objects moved together.</p><p><strong>For Korean art history</strong>, the discussion of Sŏkkuram (石窟庵) is especially valuable. Wong does not reduce it to a copy of Tang models: the sanctuary becomes a creative synthesis of the Bodhgayā prototype, the Avataṃsaka universe and architectural and iconographic elements adapted locally. Korea, however, remains less fully developed than China and Japan in the book.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="reperes"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">04 · Key references</div><h2>Sites, monuments, works and people to remember</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><ul class="book-report__entities"><li><strong>Xuanzang (玄奘)</strong><span>His return from India in 645 with texts, relics and images opens the book’s narrative. His translation, building and image-reproduction activities demonstrate how a monk could become a major agent of visual change.</span></li><li><strong>Bodhgayā and the Mahābodhi Temple</strong><span>The Buddha seated in bhūmisparśa mudrā became a prestigious prototype transmitted to China and eventually Korea. Its authority came from both sacred place and iconographic form.</span></li><li><strong>Chang’an (長安) and Luoyang (洛陽)</strong><span>The Tang capitals are the chief laboratories of the cosmopolitanism studied here: monasteries, translation bureaus, international monks, workshops and imperial patronage concentrated the production of new models.</span></li><li><strong>Wu Zhao (武曌) and Longmen (龍門)</strong><span>Her reign joined Buddhist sovereignty, Avataṃsaka, colossal monuments and iconographic programs. The great Vairocana at Longmen is a key landmark in the relationship between image and power.</span></li><li><strong>Dōji (道慈) and Daianji (大安寺)</strong><span>Dōji embodies the Japanese monk who studied in China and then participated in reshaping Nara Buddhism. The rebuilding of Daianji allows Wong to trace the transfer of an ideal monastery and new artistic subjects.</span></li><li><strong>Tōdaiji (東大寺)</strong><span>The Great Buddha Vairocana and its program show how the court of Shōmu and Kōmyō reworked models associated with Wu Zhao into a Japanese expression of the Buddhist state.</span></li><li><strong>Jianzhen (鑑真) and Tōshōdaiji (唐招提寺)</strong><span>Jianzhen’s journey to Japan reveals the movement of relics, ritual objects, sculptural techniques, ordination practices and devotional forms in the later eighth century.</span></li><li><strong>Sŏkkuram (石窟庵)</strong><span>For Grand Silla, this is the major case study: the central Buddha draws on the Bodhgayā prototype while the architectural and iconographic ensemble transforms models from several regions into a new local program.</span></li></ul></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="these"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">05 · Argument</div><h2>The author’s thesis or guiding idea</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p class="book-report__thesis">The East Asian International Buddhist Art Style of ca. 645–770 did not emerge through abstract diffusion from a center to passive peripheries. It took shape within a cosmopolitan environment of Buddhist-state ideology and court patronage, then traveled through identifiable agents—pilgrim-monks, foreign clerics, patrons, immigrants and itinerant craftspeople—and through great monasteries that structured their networks. Its genuinely international character lies in the fact that transmitted forms were selected, adopted and transformed locally.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="changement"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">06 · Significance</div><h2>What this book changes in our understanding</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><p>After this book, simply speaking of “Tang influence” is no longer enough. The stronger questions are: who carried the image or practice, through which institution, in what ritual and political setting, and what changed when it arrived? This shift restores people, routes and places of production to the center of art history.</p><p>The book also changes how Sŏkkuram and Grand Silla art can be viewed. Similarity to China does not imply passive reception. The “transmission-transformation” model instead explains how prestigious prototypes—Bodhgayā, Avataṃsaka, protective imagery—were recomposed into new local programs.</p></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="limites"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">07 · Critical reading</div><h2>Limits of the book</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><div class="book-report__limits">Wong explicitly states that the book is not a general history of Tang or Nara Buddhist art. Focusing on a few “prime movers” makes the argument precise but necessarily excludes many participants. The China–Japan axis dominates; Korea receives more selective treatment, especially through Sŏkkuram and continental exchange. The emphasis on courts, the Buddhist state and great monasteries also privileges elite production; the author acknowledges that a fuller account would need more attention to lay devotion, doctrinal developments and regional variation. The Dōji chapters also face a thinner contemporary source base and conflicting later accounts. Finally, the category of an “international style” is a powerful explanatory model, but it should not flatten the local diversity that Wong herself recognizes.</div></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="public"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">08 · Audience</div><h2>Who is this book for?</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><div class="book-report__audience"><div><strong>Beginner</strong><span>Not the best first introduction to East Asian Buddhist art. Some prior knowledge of Tang, Nara, Grand Silla and Mahāyāna Buddhism is helpful.</span></div><div><strong>Student</strong><span>Excellent for learning how to build a transregional art history that connects style, ritual, institutions, mobility and political power.</span></div><div><strong>Researcher</strong><span>A valuable reference for China–Japan circulation, agency, Avataṃsaka, state Buddhism, great monasteries and artistic transfer.</span></div><div><strong>Korean art specialist</strong><span>Important for placing Sŏkkuram and Grand Silla within a connected East Asian system, while remembering that Korea is not the book’s primary focus.</span></div></div></div></div></section>
<section class="book-report__section" id="verdict"><div class="book-report__shell"><div class="book-report__section-head"><div class="book-report__number">09 · Conclusion</div><h2>Verdict</h2></div><div class="book-report__content"><div class="book-report__verdict"><div class="book-report__verdict-label">Recommendation level</div><strong>Essential reading — for understanding how Buddhist forms become “international”</strong><p>One of the most useful books for moving from a history of “influences” to a history of circulation, agents and transformation. Its strength lies in joining art history, Buddhist studies and political history. For work on Tang, Nara, Grand Silla, Avataṃsaka or the mobility of religious forms, it offers an exceptionally productive methodological framework.</p></div></div></div></section>
